title: Mumbai Bans Rockets and Aerial Firecrackers Until November 25 After Diwali Fires
excerpt: The Disaster Management Authority order covers rooftops, balconies and slum pockets across BMC limits after three major fires on Diwali night. No casualties were reported.
body:
• Mumbai's Disaster Management Authority has banned rockets and aerial firecrackers across all Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) limits until 11:59 p.m. on November 25, after three major fires on Diwali night.
  • The order covers public and private spaces alike, including rooftops, terraces, balconies and slum pockets. Ground-level firecrackers are not covered by the ban as reported.
  • The three fires — at a Dongri chawl, an Andheri garage and a Vidyavihar commercial building — damaged huts, shops and offices but caused no casualties. Thane district has separately banned aerial crackers until January 8.

Mumbai has banned rockets and aerial firecrackers across the city until November 25, after three major fires broke out in different parts of the city on Diwali night, civic officials said on Monday.

The ban was imposed by the Mumbai Disaster Management Authority under the Disaster Management Act, according to PTI reporting cited by Mint. India Today reported that the order, issued by Additional Municipal Commissioner Prajakta Lavangare-Varma as chairperson of the authority, runs from November 9 until 11:59 p.m. on November 25, 2026, and applies across BMC limits, including rooftops, balconies, terraces, parking areas and slum pockets. The concern, officials said, is that rockets and aerial crackers fly into the sky and land on rooftops, balconies and other combustible material.

Three fires in one night

The first fire broke out at Haji Kasam Chawl, a row tenement on Dr Maheshwari Road in Dongri, at around 10 p.m. on Sunday. What began as a Level-I fire was upgraded to Level-II, and firefighters worked for more than nine hours, concluding operations at 7:23 a.m. on Monday. Several huts and shops were damaged as the fire spread to electrical wiring, wooden furniture, LPG cylinders, chemical drums and tarpaulin sheets.

A second Level-II fire was reported at a garage on Marol Military Road in Andheri, near a school, at 10:51 p.m. It was extinguished at 3:50 a.m. after nearly five hours. The third incident, at Skyline Vida, a 10-storey commercial building near Jolly Gymkhana in Vidyavihar, began at 11:56 p.m.; flames spread from the seventh to the tenth floor, and the fire was put out at 5:55 a.m. No casualties were reported in any of the three incidents.

"Let us celebrate responsibly and ensure that our festivities do not come at the cost of someone else's safety."

— Ritu Tawde, Mayor of Mumbai

What the ban does and does not cover

The order targets the firecrackers that leave the ground — rockets and aerial crackers — rather than firecrackers as a whole. Mayor Ritu Tawde, in a video appeal, urged residents to celebrate Diwali responsibly, referred to the Bombay High Court's directions against bursting firecrackers on footpaths and in public places, and warned that rockets and aerial crackers can enter homes, damage property and put lives at risk. She asked residents to keep any celebrations away from residential buildings and occupied structures.

Mumbai is not acting alone. Thane district, where 50 residents were rescued from a high-rise fire, has banned aerial rockets and similar firecrackers for a longer period, until January 8, according to PTI reporting.

What residents should know

For households in Mumbai, the practical position until November 25 is simple: no rockets and no aerial firecrackers anywhere within BMC limits, including a building's own terrace or balcony. In an emergency, the Mumbai Fire Brigade can be reached on 101 and the BMC helpline on 1916, numbers published in civic reporting on the ban.
